plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: In its native habitat the poinsettia grows as a tall, leggy shrub. It is topped with flame-red bracts that look like petals. The true flowers are tiny golden-yellow cups clustered in the middle of each red rosette. They glow against the dark green leaves.
plants.location: Mexico, its native range, and warm frost-free regions such as Central America
plants.funFact: The showy red parts are modified leaves called bracts. The real flowers are the small yellow cyathia in the center. The plant turns red as the long nights of late autumn arrive.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: This glossy-leaved evergreen shrub lights up the autumn garden with delicate, open flowers. They have silky petals and a boss of golden stamens. Unlike its fussier spring-blooming cousins, it keeps flowering as the days cool and the first chill of winter arrives. It often scatters the ground with fallen petals.
plants.bloomingSeason: Autumn into early winter (typically October or November through December or January)
plants.location: Native to Japan; widely grown in temperate gardens across Asia, Europe and North America
plants.funFact: Sasanqua camellias are closely related to the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. They are among the first camellias to bloom each year, well ahead of the spring-flowering japonica types.

plants.name: Jacaranda mimosifolia
plants.description: In late spring, jacaranda trees across the Southern Hemisphere are covered in clouds of lavender-blue, trumpet-shaped flowers. Fern-like foliage casts dappled shade beneath them. As the blossoms drop, they carpet pavements and lawns in purple. By late November the show is winding down in many places.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late October through November in Australia, with peak bloom in early November
plants.location: Australia, where it is widely planted as a street and park tree; native to South America
plants.funFact: Although jacarandas are planted in cities around the world, the species comes from South America. In Australia their flowering coincides with the late-spring season, which gives the trees a reputation for heralding the approach of summer.
